standards.title: Start with the three common markings
standards.description: One tire may show all three markings. They describe the same size, but their precision and use differ: check the rim with ETRTO first, then use inch and French markings to read packaging or sidewall information.

etrto.name: ETRTO / ISO marking
etrto.description: The format is width–bead seat diameter (BSD), both in millimetres. In 37-622, 37 is the nominal width and 622 is the BSD; check the second number first when matching a rim.

inch.name: Inch / imperial marking
inch.description: A traditional outer diameter × width format whose values are usually approximate. The same inch name can refer to different BSDs, so return to ETRTO when reading an older tire or package.

french.name: French marking
french.description: An outer diameter × width format followed by a letter code, such as 700 × 35C. C identifies a rim-diameter category; it is common on road and gravel tires but does not replace ETRTO/BSD.

availability.title: Common marking reference
availability.description: These entries are grouped by common rim-size names. Expand a group to find the names used for the same size.

mystery.title: Why 28 inch and 29 inch can both be 622
mystery.sameDescription: Both 28 inch touring or road tires and 29 inch MTB tires can use a 622 mm BSD. Width, frame clearance, and the exact tire construction still determine fitment.
mystery.contextBody: 28 inches is the traditional European size for touring bikes. 29 inches is a marketing term introduced in the US for voluminous MTB tires that have an approximate outer diameter of 29 inches when mounted.
mystery.realityBody: Both designations are imprecise. A narrow 28 inch road tire can be about 26 inches in outer diameter, while a wide 60 mm or larger MTB tire can be almost 30 inches.
